title: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: The North Star Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Business problem The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick. Behind that single experience, several specialized sub-agents work together: the Performance Insights Agent for territory-scoped revenue and performance, the Customer Insights Agent for customer intelligence, the Data Insights Agent for text-to-SQL over foundational datasets, and direct dashboard access. Answers are scoped to each user’s territory and role-level security. Field teams use these answers to assist in planning account strategy, prepare for customer meetings, so the numbers must be right. The most damaging failure is not a crash. It’s a fluent, confident answer that is quietly wrong. Before launch, when we evaluated the Customer Insights Agent, we found exactly that: It reported $410.08 of a customer’s three-month revenue on a service as “$410.08 Million.” It reported Sales Revenue labeled as Sales Revenue excluding Adjustments. It offered an Annual Recurring Revenue estimate that appeared nowhere in the data. It presented its own calculations as sourced facts. Through the different runs, monitoring stayed green. It told us the system had responded, not whether the answer was right. Had these errors shipped uncaught, the field would have paid for them. A seller who repeats an inflated figure can lose credibility with the customer. This is exactly why we caught it before launch. The risk doesn’t end at launch: it grows with every new agent and every change to data, prompts, code, or models. It also grows without any release, because upstream pipelines refresh the data every week. Coordinated releases introduce a related risk: when a data change, a tool change, and a paired prompt update are meant to ship together but land apart, the system runs mismatched until all changes catch up. In one pre-production test, that mismatch window by itself dropped the pass rate from 78 percent to 38 percent. To catch failures like these, before every release and continuously in production, we need a framework that can show whether answers are grounded and correct, and trace each failure back to its root cause in the data, the prompt, or the agent’s code. At AWS, the Sales, Marketing, and Global Services (SMGS) Operations team developed a production multi-agent system serving AWS Field Sales worldwide. It serves two distinct audiences. For field sales teams, it replaces hours of manual data analysis with on-demand, conversational intelligence, helping sellers understand the health of their business, surface risks and opportunities, and take action faster. For leadership, it powers business management cadences including Weekly Business Reviews (WBRs), surfacing the signals that matter across the portfolio without requiring manual report preparation. title: Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS
abstract: Reflection AI introduced Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks such as maintaining code, using tools, interpreting results, and completing multi-step workflows. The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process. In this post, we explain Reflection’s vision and show how you can deploy Beam on AWS. Start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed path. When you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure, use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM. We also explain how Beam’s 501 billion total parameters shape checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while its 23 billion active parameters influence per-token compute. At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). Reflection’s vision for open intelligence Reflection’s mission is to make intelligence open and accessible to all through open model weights, published research, and open source software. Its full AI stack spans models, core software, production infrastructure, and applications. Beam brings this approach to developers building software engineering and agentic systems. About Reflection Beam Beam is a sparse mixture-of-experts model for resolving software issues, modifying code, calling tools, and acting on intermediate results. It has 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens. Reflection releases Beam’s weights through Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam 1.0 is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants. These formats provide different memory footprints and hardware compatibility. You can deploy the model with the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or inspect and customize the model with SGLang or vLLM in your AWS environment. Understand the deployment architecture Choose the serving path that meets your control and scaling requirements. Start with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint when you want an AWS managed model package, endpoint, and invocation API without operating Kubernetes. Use JumpStart on HyperPod Inference when you want the AWS managed container and model configuration on a HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use SGLang or vLLM on HyperPod Inference when you need to control the serving image, runtime arguments, quantization, or distributed execution. Size the deployment for checkpoint storage, weight memory, KV cache, context length, batching, runtime overhead, and the supported parallelism. Define the expected concurrency and latency targets, then configure replicas, caching, routing, and autoscaling from measured workload behavior. The JumpStart real-time path packages the model, container, and endpoint behind a managed deployment workflow. The HyperPod path exposes the cluster and serving runtime so that you can control distributed execution, caching, routing, and scaling. title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
abstract: Prasanna Vijayanathan , Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded. This post is about that search for the needle. The Four hours before a fix Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it? As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner. The MELT Layer “What caused the issue?” Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to. MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system. The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer: What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out The timeline of an investigation So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again? A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover. The disagreement underneath The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow. It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle. Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas , our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found. This Week in AI: Expanding the Possibilities
abstract: New AI tools are making business data easier to explore. They’re also giving researchers new ways to study disease outbreaks and physical systems. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined developments from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, new research on the economics of robotics, and how scientists are using AI to tackle difficult problems. New AI tools put more capabilities directly in users’ hands OpenAI’s new Intelligent UI feature lets ChatGPT generate visual explanations and interactive tools directly in conversations. With the launch of MCP Events , supported connected applications can notify ChatGPT when something happens. If a user has asked ChatGPT to watch for that event, it can follow their instructions and take requested actions without waiting for another prompt. Anthropic’s Claude Dashboards brings natural-language queries and interactive visualizations to company data. Claude Motion adds another visual capability, turning reports and charts into editable animations. Self-service dashboards can create a range of problems though. For example, employees may reference incomplete data or apply different definitions to the same metric, then share their results as authoritative. As more employees take on exploratory analysis, BI teams will need to expand their role by maintaining reliable data and shared definitions, setting clear governance and access rules, helping employees interpret results responsibly, and monitoring how dashboards are used. Beyond the big two, Mistral previewed Large 4 , a trillion-parameter open-weight model designed for coding, agents, and multimodal tasks. The company plans to release the model’s weights soon, giving developers access to another large model for building and running AI applications. As AI agents gain access to more applications and company data, organizations will need clearer rules about what those agents can access and when humans should intervene. Recent internal tests at Anthropic showed how difficult it can be to control agents once they have access to external systems. The company reported cases of Claude circumventing restrictions, including copying server files and submitting fabricated forms, and subsequently restricted live internet access in internal tests until they’re better able to monitor their systems. OpenAI also announced plans for text watermarking in the EU , though editing and short passages can make watermarks difficult to detect reliably. Robotics research puts automation forecasts in perspective A new Anthropic study offered a useful counterpoint to predictions of widespread job displacement. Researchers found that existing robots could perform tasks accounting for roughly 34% of US work hours, but doing so would be cost competitive for just 0.3% of work hours. Most of these tasks take place in structured environments such as factories, where robots can operate more reliably than in unpredictable settings. When researchers combined the potential exposure of cognitive work to language models with physical work exposed to robotics, the share of work hours potentially affected reached 81%. For employers and policymakers, exposure figures help identify which tasks could change, but they don’t predict how many jobs automation will eliminate. Deployment costs, working conditions, and the need for human judgment will influence how quickly employers adopt these technologies . As we discussed during the audience Q&A, jobs are already changing, particularly in technical fields, even without evidence of massive displacement. For now, employers may get more value from helping workers develop new skills than from planning around speculative job-loss forecasts. AI is opening new avenues for scientific research AI is helping researchers tackle problems in mathematics, biology, space, and public health. title: Code Review After Code Gets Cheap
abstract: In my previous article , I argued that agentic development needs enough specification to make correctness checkable. A quick prompt can get implementation started quickly, but someone still has to decide whether the result does what we wanted. I left a fairly practical question unanswered, though. Once the agent has written the code, how should we review it? You can give an agent a clear task and get back a serious implementation with tests. The build passes and the code looks reasonable. Now somebody has to approve the pull request, and that person has roughly the same amount of time they had before code generation became cheap. Reading every changed line is one way to approach this. But if each increase in generated code requires a similar increase in human inspection, review will keep limiting how many changes we can accept. We need a way to decide where that inspection is worth the effort. My approach is to make evidence a condition of accepting agent-generated code. Agree on the intended behavior and the expected blast radius before implementation starts. Then use the evidence to check for drift and decide which parts of the code need direct inspection. So far, that may sound like test-driven development. But what happens when every test passes and the agent has added behavior nobody asked for? A small diff can have a large blast radius Let’s use a small fictional example. Suppose we are adding an approval step to a refund service. Refunds above €100 require approval from an authorized employee before the service sends the payment request. Exactly €100 does not require this additional approval. The existing rules about who can request a refund continue to apply. An agent implements the approval step and adds tests. While updating the payment integration, it also adds retries after a timeout. That seems reasonable enough. Network calls fail, and retrying them is a familiar engineering practice. But a timeout leaves us with another question. The provider may have issued the refund before its response was lost. Sending the request again could issue a second refund. Whether that can happen depends on how the provider handles repeated requests and how our code uses that behavior. The approval feature may be correct while the added retry introduces a separate problem. I can see a human review focusing only on the requested feature and easily missing the new decision about payment behavior. By blast radius, I mean how far the effects of a mistake can spread. If the agent puts the retry in a shared payment client, it may affect every refund, including those below the approval threshold. The change now reaches beyond the feature we asked for. Counting the changed lines won’t tell us that. Treat blast radius as a review criterion on its own. Establish which operations a change is allowed to affect, then check whether the implementation stays within that boundary. Also consider how hard a mistake would be to undo. Deploying the previous version won’t recover money that has already been refunded twice. Look for drift in both directions This is the kind of drift I want a review process to expose. We need to check that the requested behavior exists and examine additional behavior that could affect the system. There is an established name for following these relationships in both directions: bidirectional traceability. NASA’s software engineering guidance describes tracing requirements through implementation and verification, including finding functionality that has no parent requirement. I think that the basic idea translates quite well to an ordinary pull request. For each important requirement, we should be able to find the implementation and the checks that support it. Looking back from the implementation, we should be able to explain why a change to behavior belongs in this pull request. An extra private method will usually need little discussion. title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
abstract: More than 5 million people around the world have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which cells in the retinas die off. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones. The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors. BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology. BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable . CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom. BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye. SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery. Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats. Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
abstract: I. Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer. When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress. So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly. A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times . And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer. For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring. At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point. “St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
abstract: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats. I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it. That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though. I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin. Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced. Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider. title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
abstract: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. title: Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design
abstract: This article is brought to you by COMSOL . These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distributi on centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible. To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations. The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance. Laser Who? The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness. The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process. Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.” R&D Workflow for Multiscale Model and App The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started. “Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app. After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior. After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model. title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
abstract: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives. Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior. Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect , communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior . title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
abstract: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. title: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
abstract: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories. Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform , for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win. This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates. Read full article Comments

title: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft's promises
abstract: Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn't feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly. The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both. title: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
abstract: Android was designed for phones, but that hasn't stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps. Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems. For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. title: 실행은 도메인별로, 문맥은 한 레포에
abstract: 들어가며 안녕하세요, 토스 Data Warehouse 팀의 Data Analytics Engineer 김문수입니다. 이 글에서는 데이터 웨어하우스(DW) 마트를 만드는 중앙 DW Airflow를 멈추지 않고, 도메인별 DW Airflow와 dbt 기반의 선언적 파이프라인으로 옮겨 온 과정을 공유하려고 합니다. 새 플랫폼은 팀 안에서 이를 ‘뉴타운’이라고 부르고 있습니다. 얼마 전 코딩 에이전트에게 "이 테이블 어디서 만들어져?"라고 물었습니다. 한참 코드를 뒤지던 에이전트의 답은 이랬습니다. "적재 주체는 코드에 없어 확인할 수 없습니다." 맞는 말입니다. 정말로 코드에 없었기 때문이죠. 이 글은 그 답을 코드에 적어 넣기까지의 이야기입니다. 그 과정에서 토스 광고 도메인의 DAG 코드는 2,794줄에서 100줄 이 되었고, 테이블 순서를 손으로 잇던 >> 180줄은 0줄 이 되었습니다. 파이프라인 시간도 4시간에서 2시간 30분 으로 줄었습니다. DW Airflow 하나에 DAG 400여 개 토스에는 용도와 팀에 따라 운영하는 Airflow가 여럿 있습니다. 이 글에서 다루는 건 그중 DW 마트를 만드는 DW Airflow입니다. DW 마트에는 광고, 쇼핑, 결제, 금융 등 도메인 팀이 각자 관리하는 도메인 마트와, 중앙 DW팀이 관리하는 마트가 있습니다. 중앙 DW팀은 전사 공통 마트뿐 아니라, 어느 도메인에도 딱 떨어지지 않아 주인이 애매한 마트까지 맡고 있습니다. 그런데 이 마트 파이프라인이 도메인과 상관없이 전부 DW Airflow 클러스터 하나에서 돌고 있었습니다. DAG 파일로 세면 400개가 넘습니다. 한 클러스터에 모여 있다 보니 문제가 몇 가지 있었습니다. 한 도메인의 배치가 몰리면 다른 도메인의 배치까지 밀렸고, 파이프라인 하나를 고치려면 다른 도메인이 어떻게 돌고 있는지까지 알아야 했습니다. 비슷한 로직도 표준 없이 여기저기 복사돼 있었습니다. 매일 겪는 불편은 조금 더 구체적이었습니다. 테이블 하나를 이해하려면 다섯 군데를 열어야 했습니다. 어느 DAG에서 어떤 순서로 도는지: DAG 파일 어떻게 만드는지: SQL 파일 품질 규칙: 별도 설정 파일이나 품질 관리 시스템 테이블과 컬럼 설명: 사내 데이터 카탈로그 읽는 테이블이 어디서 만들어지는지: 원천 DB에서 적재한 테이블이면 적재 메타 관리 시스템, 다른 마트면 영향도 시스템 등 여러 사내 시스템 고쳐 쓰지 않고 옆에 새로 짓기로 했습니다 처음에는 기존 레포를 리팩토링하는 방법도 생각했습니다. 그런데 문제의 뿌리가 "클러스터 하나에 다 모여 있다"는 구조 자체라서, 코드를 아무리 정리해도 이 부분은 해결이 안 됩니다. 그렇다고 전사 배치를 한 번에 새 플랫폼으로 옮기는 건 너무 위험합니다. 문제가 생기면 대응하기가 꽤 까다로워요. 돌이킬 수 있으면서 간편한 방식을 원했습니다. 그래서 기존 시스템 옆에 새 시스템을 짓고, 기능을 하나씩 옮긴 뒤 옮긴 부분만 기존 시스템에서 걷어내는 방식을 택했습니다. 이걸 부르는 이름이 있을 것 같아 찾아보니 Strangler Fig 방식이라고 하더라고요. 교살 무화과나무가 숙주 나무를 감싸며 자라다가 결국 기존 나무를 대체하는 자연현상에서 유래했다고 합니다. (이름이 무서운 나무네요.) 아무튼 기존 파이프라인은 마지막 순간까지 그대로 돌고, 옮기다 문제가 생기면 언제든 되돌릴 수 있습니다. 옮기는 단위를 도메인으로 잡았기 때문에, 언제, 얼마나 옮길지는 도메인 팀이 정할 수 있었습니다. 같은 데이터를 하루에 두 번 만들었습니다 플랫폼이 어느정도 만들어졌을 때, 적당한 마이그레이션 대상을 찾고 있었는데요. 마침 찾은 이 마트 DAG은 주인이 따로 없고, 마지막 변경이 1년이 넘었고, TASK의 수도 적당했습니다. 7월 말에 이 마트를 옮겨 둔 도메인의 main DAG에 13시 대기 sensor와 이 마트의 트리거를 추가했습니다. 기존 파이프라인은 평소처럼 새벽에 돌고, 뉴타운은 같은 날 13시에 같은 데이터를 한 번 더 만듭니다. 같은 데이터를 하루에 두 번 만드는 건 낭비 같지만, 가장 싼 보험이었습니다. 이렇게 3주 동안 두 결과를 비교했습니다. 8월 20일에 검증이 끝났다고 보고, 13시 대기를 빼서 새벽에 돌게 하는 PR을 머지했습니다. 그런데 같은 날 저녁 revert했습니다. 문제가 생긴 건 아니고, 기존 파이프라인 쪽 준비가 더 필요했기 때문입니다. 기존 DW Airflow에는 테이블간의 audit 기반으로 만든 영향도를 보고 앞 단계를 기다리는 sensor가 있어서, 이 마트를 뉴타운 쪽 결과로 바라보게 바꾸는 작업을 따로 해야 했습니다. 그래서 다음 주로 미뤘습니다. revert 커밋 메시지는 ‘다음주에 하는걸로’ 한 줄이었고, 실제로 8월 24일에 다시 머지했습니다. 그동안 기존 파이프라인은 계속 새벽에 돌고 있었으니 데이터를 쓰는 쪽에서는 아무 일도 없었습니다. 한 번에 옮기는 방식이었다면 이 일정 조정은 꽤 큰 롤백 작업이 됐을 겁니다. 광고 도메인을 옮길 때도 같은 방식으로 두 파이프라인을 나란히 돌리며 결과를 비교한 뒤 넘겼습니다. 반대로 하지 않기로 한 것도 있습니다. Spark 잡은 dbt로 바꾸지 않았고, Jenkins 잡도 당장 없애지 않고 이어 쓰되 새로 만드는 것만 막았습니다. 다 할 수는 있는 일이지만, 전부 새 방식으로 바꾸려고 하면 이주가 늦어지고 두 플랫폼을 같이 운영하는 기간만 길어집니다. 같은 이유로 기존의 모델 레이어 구성 방식을 바꾸는 것도 이관 이후에 하는 걸 권장했어요. 도메인별 클러스터와 dbt 새 플랫폼에서는 DW Airflow를 도메인별로 나눴습니다. 도메인마다 자기 DW Airflow 클러스터를 갖는 구조로, 지금은 ads, foundation, finops, fmd, dw-core까지 5개 클러스터가 있습니다. 다만 기존 파이프라인을 대규모로 옮겨 온 건 아직 광고(ads) 한 곳이고, 나머지는 새로 만드는 마트나 옮기기 위한 준비 위주로 쓰이고 있습니다. 도메인 팀이 자기 파이프라인을 책임지려면, 다른 도메인의 배포나 장애에 흔들리지 않는 실행 환경이 있어야 한다고 봤습니다. 코드는 레포 하나에 두고, 공통 모듈은 플랫폼팀이, 도메인 디렉토리는 각 도메인 팀이 관리합니다. 물론 공통 모듈에 기여하는 건 누구나 할 수 있습니다. 변환 로직은 Impala에 직접 날리던 쿼리에서 dbt 모델로 옮겼습니다. dbt는 SELECT 문만 적으면 테이블 생성과 적재를 대신 해 주고, 모델 사이의 의존 관계를 그래프로 관리해 주는 도구입니다. dbt 모델을 Airflow task로 펼치는 데는 흔히 쓰는 Cosmos를 썼고, 모델 하나가 task 하나가 됩니다. dbt만으로는 Spark 잡이나 다른 클러스터의 테이블을 기다리는 sensor를 표현할 수 없어서, 선언만 해 두면 이런 task와 의존성을 자동으로 만들어 주는 wrapper를 따로 만들었습니다. 이 wrapper가 실제로 무엇을 읽고 무엇을 만드는지는 아래 ‘나머지는 yml에’ 문단에서 보여 드리겠습니다. 클러스터를 나누니 새로운 문제도 생겼습니다. 클러스터 하나일 때는 손쉽게 해결됐던 DAG 간 의존이, 클러스터를 건너는 의존이 된 것입니다. 이건 두 가지로 풀었습니다. 도메인마다 스케줄을 가진 main DAG를 하나만 두고 나머지 DAG는 main이 trigger하게 해서, 모두 같은 날짜를 공유하게 했습니다. 기존 DW Airflow에서도 쓰던 패턴이라 팀원들이 익숙하게 받아들일 수 있었습니다. 그리고 다른 곳에서 만드는 테이블은 만들어지는 방식에 따라 기다리는 방법을 나눴습니다. 원천 DB에서 적재하는 테이블은 적재 상태가 적재 시스템의 백엔드 서버에 메타로 기록되고 있어서, ‘오늘 적재됐는가’를 그 기록에서 직접 확인할 수 있었습니다. 기존 DW Airflow에서 만드는 마트는 그 테이블을 만드는 Airflow task가 끝났는지를 봅니다. SQL에는 로직만 남겼습니다 기존 SQL과 옮긴 뒤의 SQL을 간단히 비교하면 이렇습니다. (예시를 위해 단순화했습니다.) insert overwrite 같은 적재 구문은 사라지고, 읽는 테이블 이름이 ref() 로 바뀝니다. 비즈니스 로직은 그대로입니다. 대

title: 토스뱅크가 패키지를 관리하는 방식 #2: 토스뱅크 패키지의 세 가지 기준
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스뱅크에서 패키지 개발 환경을 개선하고 있는 기술그룹입니다. 패키지를 사용하는 쪽(이하 호스트)에서는 패키지 코드가 어떤 브라우저까지 지원하는지, 패키지 개발 중 사용하던 API를 실행 환경에서도 쓸 수 있는지 따로 살펴봐야 했어요. 호스트에서 패키지의 원본 소스 코드를 확인하기도 어려웠어요. 이 문제를 해결하기 위해 패키지가 갖춰야 할 기준을 정했어요. 그리고 각 기준을 충족하려면 무엇이 필요한지 살펴보고, 그에 맞는 빌드 도구와 설정을 선택하기로 했어요. 기준은 세 가지예요. 안정성 : 호스트가 지원하는 실행 환경에서 안정적으로 동작해야 해요. 예측 가능성 : 배포 후에도 원본 코드의 의도가 유지되어야 해요. 디버깅 편의성 : 사용처에서 쉽게 디버깅할 수 있어야 해요. 호스트가 지원하는 실행 환경에서 안정적으로 동작해야 해요 토스뱅크의 각 서비스는 자신의 지원 범위에 맞춰 패키지를 항상 트랜스파일해요. 그럼 최신 문법을 모두 사용해도 호스트 런타임에 문제가 없다고 보장할 수 있을까요? 문법은 호스트의 트랜스파일러가 해당 문법 변환을 지원해야 하고, API는 실행 환경에서 제공하거나 폴리필로 추가해야 해요. 예를 들어 rolldown의 문법 변환 관련 이슈 에서는 당시 oxc가 ES2025의 일부 정규식 문법을 구형 환경용으로 변환하지 못한다는 점을 짚었어요. 즉 최종 호스트가 낮은 target 을 지정하더라도 도구가 지원하지 않는 변환까지 수행되지는 않는 거예요. 폴리필에도 한계가 있어요. 예를 들어 Proxy 는 이를 지원하지 않는 엔진에서 폴리필만으로 전체 동작을 구현할 수 없어요. 폴리필 라이브러리를 추가하는 것만으로 모든 API를 사용할 수 있게 되는 것은 아니에요. 따라서 문법은 호스트의 변환 도구가 처리할 수 있는지, API는 대상 브라우저 또는 호스트의 폴리필이 제공할 수 있는지를 각각 확인해야 해요. 트랜스파일링을 호스트에 맡기더라도 호환성 문제는 패키지 개발 단계에서 미리 확인해야 해요. 그래서 호스트의 API 지원 범위를 타입 검사에 반영했어요. 다만 TypeScript 설정만으로 호환성을 모두 확인할 수는 없으므로, 실제 API 지원 여부와 필요한 문법 변환이 가능한지도 확인해야 해요. 배포 후에도 원본 코드의 의도가 유지되어야 해요 호스트는 자신의 실행 환경에 맞춰 패키지 코드를 변환하고 번들링해요. 저희는 이 작업을 호스트에 맡기고, 패키지 빌드에서는 원본의 문법과 모듈 구조를 최대한 유지하기로 했어요. 문법 변환은 호스트에 맡겨요 패키지를 사용하는 서비스마다 지원하는 브라우저와 런타임이 달라요. 따라서 같은 패키지 코드라도 호스트에 따라 필요한 문법 변환이 달라질 수 있어요. 예를 들어 user?.name 을 Optional Chaining을 지원하지 않는 환경에 맞춰 변환하면 다음처럼 바뀔 수 있어요. 이 상태로 패키지를 배포하면 Optional Chaining을 지원하는 호스트도 변환된 코드를 받게 돼요. 문법에 따라서는 호환성을 위한 함수가 추가되기도 해요. 패키지에서 문법을 미리 낮추면 호스트에 필요하지 않은 코드가 포함되고, 원본과 결과물의 차이도 커져요. 그래서 저희는 패키지의 JavaScript 문법을 유지하고, 실행 환경에 맞춘 문법 변환은 호스트에 맡기기로 했어요. 호스트가 자신의 지원 범위에 맞춰 필요한 변환을 적용하도록 했어요. 모듈 구조도 유지해 전달해요 패키지를 빌드할 때 미리 번들링하면, 원본에서 나눠 둔 파일의 경계가 달라질 수 있어요. 프레임워크가 파일 단위로 코드를 처리하는 경우에는 이 차이가 실제 동작에도 영향을 줄 수 있어요. 예를 들어 Next.js App Router에서는 'use client' 를 선언한 파일이 클라이언트 코드의 경계가 돼요. 이 선언이 있는 Counter.tsx 와 선언이 없는 formatPrice.ts 가 분리돼 있다면, Server Component에서도 formatPrice 를 가져와 호출할 수 있어요. 하지만 두 파일을 하나로 번들링하고 전체에 'use client' 를 적용하면, formatPrice 도 클라이언트 코드로 처리돼 같은 방식으로 호출할 수 없어요. 번들링 과정에서도 이런 경계를 유지할 수 있어요. 다만 패키지 빌드에서 파일별 지시문의 적용 범위까지 고려해야 하고, 이를 위한 설정도 관리해야 해요. 그래서 저희는 원본의 모듈 구조를 유지해 배포하기로 했어요. 호스트가 파일별 지시문과 모듈 경계를 해석할 수 있도록 전달하고, 최종 번들링은 호스트에 맡겼어요. 패키지 빌드에서는 TypeScript를 JavaScript로 변환하고, 실행 환경에 맞춘 문법 변환과 최종 번들링은 호스트가 담당하도록 했어요. 사용처에서 쉽게 디버깅할 수 있어야 해요 패키지가 예상과 다르게 동작하면 사용하는 서비스에서도 원인을 파악할 수 있어야 해요. 함수가 어떤 조건에서 오류를 던지는지, 옵션을 생략하면 어떻게 동작하는지 확인하려면 타입 선언과 문서만으로는 부족할 수 있어요. 이때 가장 빠른 방법은 원본 코드를 직접 확인하는 거예요. 그래서 에디터에서 패키지의 원본 코드를 바로 확인할 수 있도록 declaration sourcemap을 지원하기로 했어요. declaration sourcemap은 .d.ts 의 각 선언을 원본 소스의 해당 위치와 연결해 주는 파일이에요. 이 파일과 원본 파일을 설치된 패키지에 포함하면, 사용하는 쪽에서도 IDE에서 클릭 한 번으로 d.ts 대신 실제 구현을 확인할 수 있어요. 마치며 호스트의 지원 범위에 맞춰 패키지를 개발하고, 문법과 모듈 구조를 유지해 배포하도록 기준을 정했어요. 사용하는 쪽에서는 자신의 환경에 맞춰 문법 변환과 번들링을 진행하고, 문제가 생기면 설치된 패키지의 원본 구현을 바로 확인할 수 있도록 했어요. 저희 기술그룹은 안정성, 예측 가능성, 디버깅 편의성을 기준으로 패키지를 만드는 쪽과 사용하는 쪽의 역할을 정리했어요. 이 기준 덕분에 빌드 도구와 설정을 선택할 때도, 어떤 변환이 필요하고 어떤 파일을 제공해야 하는지 일관되게 판단할 수 있게 됐어요.

title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models
abstract: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.

title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) represent model activations with sparse, linearly decoded features, but the downstream effects of those features need not compose additively. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), which measure the behavioral variation left unexplained above a chosen interaction order. Under independent feature subset sampling, population SAR is exactly the normalized energy of interactions above that order and bounds coalition ordering error for the optimal low order approximation. To distinguish compositionality associated with the SAE representation from that induced by downstream computation, we compare learned SAE coordinates with sum preserving random rotations of the same selected subspace and find lower first order residuals for the learned coordinates across all 18 model and behavior settings. The coordinates are nevertheless not fully additive: pairwise terms improve held out coalition ordering in every setting and outperform parameter matched models using randomly selected third order terms. In a combined steering experiment, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. Together, these results show that SAE coordinates support comparatively compositional behavioral descriptions while faithful joint explanations and interventions still require interactions beyond individual feature effects. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/SAE-Behavioral-Compositionality.

title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research.

title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model's hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55--11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.

title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
abstract: Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities. We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.

title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

title: Equal CER, Unequal Damage: Severity-Weighted Character Error Rate for OCR
abstract: Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for OCR and vision-language models (VLMs), charges a typo as much as a wrong name. We introduce semCER, which keeps CER's alignment and denominator and charges each grapheme edit a severity from an LLM judge, with no word segmentation. Normalized CER keeps the score of a whole transcription, where it tracks readers as well as semCER or better, and semCER breaks that score down into named edits. The charges track readers' ratings edit by edit in English, Vietnamese, and Chinese and put the edits readers rate most severe near the top of a sorted list. On pairs drawn where CER and semCER disagreed, readers side with semCER more often than with normalized CER in English and Chinese, and equally often in Vietnamese. Across 16 languages, the judge charges a wrong diacritic or tone mark almost nothing in Spanish but nearly a wrong letter's severity in Telugu. Where we can count real words, a general VLM's wrong letter forms one far above chance while a classical pipeline's stays near it. We release the 61 million judged edits, the aggregated reader ratings, and the distilled scorer at https://github.com/nguyenx2t/semcer.

title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.

title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

title: Copy-Paste Language Models
abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.

title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
abstract: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.

title: PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.

title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.

title: One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation
abstract: Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness.

title: Gen4P: Video Generators are 4D Perceivers
abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.

title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.

title: Virtual Head Attention
abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank I + AB^top residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale (+0.05\% to +0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by 4times vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and 2times vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, S{=}4096). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by +0.70\,/\,+2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.

title: Speech event detector: Timestamped detection of non-verbal vocalizations and background sounds for rich speech transcription
abstract: Automatic speech recognition produces words but drops the non-verbal content of a recording: the breaths, coughs, sighs and laughter of the speaker, and the horns, music or barking around them. We describe Speech Event Detector, a 5.8-million-parameter convolutional-Transformer model that outputs probabilities every 40 ms for 54 event classes (20 speaker vocalizations and 34 background sounds), together with post-processing that converts these probabilities into timestamped events and a procedure for merging the events into a Whisper transcript. The model is trained on material drawn from seven public datasets whose labels come in incompatible forms: single detected regions, free-text tags with timestamps, temporally strong ontology labels, symbols embedded in transcripts, isolated recordings and environmental recordings. We unify them using rule-based label mapping, recover timestamps for transcript-embedded labels through CTC forced alignment, locating 6,360 of 8,620 sounds, and combine about 168 hours of real annotated training recordings with synthetic mixtures and augmentation using real background noise. Per-class thresholds for two operating profiles are tuned on real held-out recordings, and performance is estimated using two-fold cross-validation. On whole held-out recordings from four datasets, considering the 48 classes with at least ten held-out events, the sensitive profile detects an average of 49 percent of a class's events, covering 67 percent of all 9,367 events, at a macro precision of 0.30. The balanced profile achieves a macro recall of 0.37 at a precision of 0.36, with macro event F1 scores of 0.32 and 0.33, respectively. The detector runs about 39 times faster than real time on eight CPU threads.

title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from O(n^2) to O(n) via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication clip--shift--max on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel.
